questions.q: Canada has no national wine law. Which level of government writes the rules instead?
questions.exp: Each province writes its own wine rules, so VQA Ontario and the BC Wine Authority keep separate standards and the smaller provinces have arrangements of their own; a VQA mark is therefore provincial, never federal. Wine is made in at least nine provinces, with the largest concentrations in Ontario and British Columbia.

questions.q: What do the letters VQA stand for on a Canadian label?
questions.exp: Vintners Quality Alliance is the body the Court names for Canada's premium wine: a VQA mark guarantees that the grapes were grown in the province or area named, that the wine meets its grape and ripeness standards, and that it has passed a tasting panel. Ontario launched it as a voluntary standard in 1988 and wrote it into provincial law in 1999.

questions.q: Which province does the Court say produces the largest share of Canadian wine?
questions.exp: The Court puts Ontario at about half of all Canadian wine, grown along the shores of Lake Ontario and Lake Erie with the Niagara Peninsula its main viticultural area. British Columbia, with the Okanagan Valley at its heart, is the second; Quebec and Nova Scotia make far smaller amounts at the cold edge of viticulture.

questions.q: What share of Canada's icewine does the Court say is made in Ontario?
questions.exp: Ontario, and the Niagara Peninsula above all, makes about nine tenths of Canada's icewine by the Court's figure, from Vidal, Riesling and Cabernet Franc left to freeze on the vine; British Columbia makes most of the rest. The Court's Style cell opens by calling Canada the leading global producer of icewine.

questions.q: When are icewine grapes often picked, according to the Court?
opts: In the middle of the night
questions.exp: The rule asks for picking at minus 8°C or colder, and the coldest hours fall before dawn, so crews often go out in the middle of the night to pick and press the grapes while the water in them is still frozen. Only the concentrated syrup runs from the press, leaving the ice behind.

questions.q: Besides Vitis labrusca, which North American native species does the Court list among Canada's vines?
questions.exp: Vitis riparia, the riverbank grape, is native across much of eastern North America and into Canada, one of the hardiest of all vine species and a parent of many winter hardy hybrids and rootstocks. The Court's three families for Canada are vinifera, the native species labrusca and riparia, and the French and American hybrids such as Vidal; amurensis is Asian and rotundifolia belongs to the warm American south.

questions.q: Which white grape, one of the Court's Certified names for Canada, leads the plantings of British Columbia's Okanagan Valley?
questions.exp: Pinot Gris is the Okanagan's leading white, ripe and pear scented, often with a touch of sweetness, from a dry, irrigated valley that is close to desert at its southern end. The Court adds Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer and the hybrid Vidal at the Certified level to the Introductory pair of Chardonnay and Riesling.

questions.q: Which red grape on the Court's Canadian list gives fine-boned, red-fruited wines from Prince Edward County's thin soils over limestone?
questions.exp: Prince Edward County, on Lake Ontario's north-eastern shore, is so cold that growers bury the vines every November, and its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay show real tension from shallow soils over limestone. Merlot is at home in the warm southern Okanagan, and Cabernet Franc is Ontario's red success on the Niagara benches; Cabernet Sauvignon ripens only on the warmest sites.

questions.q: The Court dates Canada's twentieth-century Prohibition from 1916. In which year does it put the end?
questions.exp: Prohibition came to the provinces at different times, and in Ontario it ran from 1916 to 1927, when government liquor stores replaced it; the American ban lasted from 1920 to 1933. Its long hangover meant that no new winery licence was issued in Ontario between 1929 and 1975, when Inniskillin received one, the 1970s milestone in the Court's history row.

questions.q: Which Niagara-on-the-Lake winery, the one Canadian producer on the Court's list, received in 1975 the first new Ontario winery licence granted since 1929?
questions.exp: Inniskillin's licence of 1975 was the first Ontario had issued since 1929, after the long shadow of Prohibition had closed the door on new wineries, and it opened the modern era of Niagara wine. Its 1989 Vidal Icewine went on to win the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo in 1991; the Court prints the name as Inniskillen, and the house spells it Inniskillin.

questions.q: The Court asks for sweet and savoury pairings with icewine. Which of these dishes meets that brief best?
questions.exp: Icewine's intense sweetness and high acidity cut the richness of seared foie gras, and the salt and fat of the dish set off the wine's apricot and tropical fruit; blue cheese and gently spiced dishes work for the same reason. Raw oysters, a plain steak or a sharp salad would leave the wine tasting cloying or the food thin.

questions.q: Why does the Court say the Great Lakes help moderate the winters of Canada's vineyards?
opts: They are fed by warm rivers
They are very deep and rarely freeze
They are salty and resist ice
They lie downwind of the vineyards
questions.exp: Deep water stores summer heat and gives it back slowly, so the lakes rarely freeze and keep the shore a few degrees milder through a hard winter; in spring the cold water holds bud break back until the frost danger has passed. The Niagara Escarpment then holds the lake air over the Niagara Peninsula's vines.
